My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish baseline assumption across all three horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 43.85 likely anchored near the most recent observed price or index level, with only minimal drift expected given typical overnight or intraday mean-reversion tendencies. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 44.1, reflecting a gentle upward bias consistent with the slight positive drift seen in many equity or commodity instruments over short horizons when no strong negative catalysts are immediately visible. At the one-month horizon, the estimate rises further to 44.8, incorporating a longer runway for any underlying fundamental or momentum trend to play out, while still remaining relatively conservative in the magnitude of expected movement.

The confidence interval widths widen progressively across horizons in a manner consistent with the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 2.7 units, reflecting relatively tight short-term price bounds under normal market conditions. By one week, the interval widens to about 4.6 units, capturing the accumulation of daily volatility over several sessions. At one month, the interval spans approximately 8.6 units, acknowledging that over four or more weeks, a much broader range of macroeconomic developments, earnings announcements, sentiment shifts, and liquidity conditions can materially influence the outcome. The asymmetric upper tail at one month being slightly wider than the lower tail hints at a modest positive skew assumption.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macroeconomic data, an unexpected central bank policy shift toward greater hawkishness, or a geopolitical shock could drive prices well below the lower bounds, particularly at the one-week and one-month horizons where the intervals are still relatively contained relative to crisis-episode volatility. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst such as a stronger-than-expected earnings report, a dovish policy pivot, or a resolution of an existing geopolitical tension could push prices above the upper bounds. The one-month interval is most vulnerable to being breached because it encompasses the greatest number of scheduled risk events, including central bank meetings, economic data releases, and potential policy announcements that individually carry fat-tail implications.

Finally, I want to acknowledge that these intervals were constructed under an implicit assumption of roughly normal market conditions.
